chapters.title: Chapter 2: Trend, Support and Resistance on Currency Pairs

lessons.title: Horizontal Support and Resistance: Round Numbers and Psychological Levels on USD/INR and EUR/USD

children.text: For six straight sessions, EUR/USD pushes up toward 1.1000, stalls within a few pips of it, and slides back down. There is no company results, no RBI policy, no scheduled US data release pinning it there. It is simply a round number, and round numbers are some of the strongest, most stubborn support and resistance levels you will find anywhere in currency trading.

body.text: Round numbers act as unusually strong support and resistance in forex because of how orders actually cluster around them, stop-losses, take-profits and options strikes all pile up at whole and half figures, not because of anything special about the number itself.

children.text: As a quick reminder, support is a price level where buying has repeatedly overcome selling, and resistance is a level where selling has repeatedly overcome buying. Both work because enough traders remember the level and act on it again. What forex adds to this basic idea is a very specific reason certain levels get remembered even before any real price history has formed there: the number itself is round.
Why Round Numbers Matter So Much in Forex

markDefs.definition: Forex jargon for the whole-number part of a quote. In 95.50, the "95" is the big figure and "50" are the pips. Dealers often assume the big figure is known and quote only the pips.

children.text: Three things stack up at whole numbers, often called

, far more than at any random price. First, retail traders naturally set stop-losses and take-profits at clean numbers like ₹95.00 or 1.1000 rather than at odd values like ₹94.87. Second, NSE lists USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR options at strikes spaced around the current price, and open interest tends to build up heavily at round strikes such as ₹95.00 or ₹96.00, since round strikes are what most participants naturally trade. Third, large global banks and corporates place resting orders at round levels because they are easy to communicate and remember across trading desks. None of this requires any news event. It is simply where the orders already are.

body.caption: Not all round numbers carry equal weight

cells: Meaningful, but weaker than a whole figure

body.title: Ranking psychological strength
body.question: USD/INR is approaching four nearby levels: ₹95.75, ₹96.00, ₹95.25 and ₹95.50. Which level is most likely to act as the strongest resistance on its own, purely from round-number effects?
body.explanation: ₹96.00 is a whole figure, which draws the heaviest concentration of stop-losses, take-profits and options strikes. Half figures like ₹95.50 matter too, but less. Quarter figures like ₹95.25 and ₹95.75 carry the weakest psychological pull.

children.text: Big Figure Talk: Reading Forex Jargon

Once you know why round numbers matter, forex dealer shorthand stops being confusing. If USD/INR is trading near ₹95.40 and someone quotes "50/55," they are not giving you a full price, they are dropping the big figure because it is assumed you already know it is 95. The quote means a bid of ₹95.50 and an offer of ₹95.55. This convention exists precisely because everyone is anchored to the same round-number map of the pair.

body.title: Decoding a dealer quote
body.prompt: USD/INR is trading near ₹95.90. Dropping the big figure, a dealer quotes just the pips as "95/00", meaning a bid pip value of 95 and an offer pip value of 00. What is the offer (ask) price, in rupees?
body.explanation: An offer pip value of "00" right after a bid of "95" means the price has rolled over into the next whole rupee, so the offer is ₹96.00, not ₹95.00. Reading big-figure shorthand correctly means always checking whether the pips have rolled over into the next big figure.

children.text: A common beginner mistake is drawing a single hairline exactly at 1.1000 and expecting price to reverse there to the pip. In practice, spreads, tick-by-tick noise and the sheer weight of orders sitting just before and just after the round number mean price usually reacts somewhere in a small band around it, not at one exact value.

body.title: Illustrative EUR/USD Reacting to a Zone Around 1.1000

children.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote. Price pokes above and below 1.1000 across three separate days, at 1.0996, 1.1004 and 1.1008, before finally breaking down on day three's close and falling further on day four. Anyone who marked a single exact line at 1.1000 would have been stopped out twice by the wicks alone. Marking a zone from roughly 1.0985 to 1.1010 instead would have captured the same resistance without being shaken out by ordinary noise around the round number.

body.title: One line or a zone?
body.scenario: Sanjay draws a single horizontal line at exactly ₹95.00 on his USD/INR chart and places a sell order the instant price touches it, with a tight stop-loss just 5 paise above. Over the next week, price taps 95.00 four separate times, gets stopped out three of those times by a few paise of noise, and only the fourth touch produces the reversal he expected.
body.prompt: What should Sanjay change about how he marks and trades this level, based on how round numbers actually behave?
body.modelAnswer:
1. A round number like ₹95.00 draws heavy order clustering on both sides, so price rarely reverses at the exact figure. It typically oscillates in a small band around it first.
2. Sanjay should mark a zone, for example ₹94.90 to ₹95.10, rather than a single hairline, and treat any reaction inside that band as a test of the level.
3. His stop-loss of just 5 paise is too tight for the normal noise around a heavily traded round number and is likely to be triggered by ordinary wicks rather than a genuine break.
4. He should widen his stop beyond the zone itself, or wait for a candle to close outside the zone before acting, rather than reacting to the first touch.

body.text: The strongest levels are round numbers that also line up with a prior swing high or low from actual price history. A round number on its own is a decent level. A round number that also happens to be where price reversed twice before is a much stronger one. Chapter 5 builds on this idea properly under the name confluence.

body.title: Round Numbers and Psychological Levels: Key Terms

cards.definition: The whole-number part of a currency quote, such as the "95" in 95.50. Dealers often drop it and quote only the remaining pips.
The tendency of whole and half currency levels to act as stronger support or resistance, driven by clustering of stop-losses, take-profits and options strikes.
A price band around a level, rather than a single exact line, used to account for normal noise around heavily traded round numbers.
When multiple independent reasons, such as a round number and a prior swing high, line up at the same price, making that level more reliable.

points: Round numbers act as strong support and resistance in forex because stop-losses, take-profits and options strikes genuinely cluster around them, not because the number is special.
Whole figures like ₹95.00 or 1.1000 are stronger than half figures like ₹95.50, which are in turn stronger than quarter figures like ₹95.25.
Dealer shorthand that drops the big figure, such as quoting "50/55," assumes both sides already know which whole rupee or whole dollar level the price is near.
Mark round-number levels as zones, not exact lines, since price usually oscillates around them before genuinely breaking.
A round number is a decent level on its own. A round number that also lines up with a prior swing high or low is far stronger, an idea Chapter 5 develops fully as confluence.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not trading advice. The candlestick example is illustrative and not a live or historical quote. Support and resistance levels, including round numbers, are probabilistic tools and can fail. Always combine them with proper risk management before trading.
